original_question: For 0 < beta < 1 and q = d/(d-beta), a known result proves that if f is radial and belongs to W^{1,1}(R^d), then the uncentered fractional maximal function is weakly differentiable and satisfies ||∇M̃_beta f||_{L^q(R^d)} <= C ||∇f||_{L^1(R^d)}. Does the analogous statement hold for the centered fractional maximal operator M_beta acting on radial functions?
target_in_paper: Question 8 in Section 5 ("Fractional maximal operators"): whether the centered fractional maximal operator on radial functions satisfies the same endpoint weak differentiability and gradient estimate as the uncentered operator in Theorem 5.3.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the core mathematical content of the paper-faithful target: the endpoint range 0<\beta<1, the exponent q=d/(d-\beta), the radial Sobolev input class W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d), the known uncentered theorem used as the comparison point (Theorem 5.3), and the fact that the paper asks for the centered analogue. This is very close to the official formulation of Question 8.
missing_details: State the centered fractional maximal operator explicitly, e.g. M_\beta f(x)=\sup_{r>0} \frac{r^\beta}{|B(x,r)|}\int_{B(x,r)} |f(y)|\,dy, and clarify that the uncentered operator \widetilde M_\beta takes the supremum over balls containing x but not necessarily centered at x.
Make the ambient dimension explicit: d\ge 1 (with 0<\beta<1, hence automatically \beta<d for every integer d\ge1).
Specify the quantifier 'for every radial f\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)'.
Include the dependence of the constant as C=C(d,\beta).

Say explicitly that the desired conclusion consists of both weak differentiability of M_\beta f and the endpoint estimate \|\nabla M_\beta f\|_{L^q(\mathbb{R}^d)}\le C(d,\beta)\|\nabla f\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)}.
Indicate that this is the radial centered special case of the broader endpoint boundedness question posed just before it in Question 7.

Do not add continuity at the derivative level: in arXiv:1912.04625, Question 8 only asks whether Theorem 5.3 holds in the centered case, i.e. the weak differentiability plus bound, not a continuity statement.
refined_question: Let d\ge 1, let 0<\beta<1, and set q=d/(d-\beta). For f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^d), define the centered fractional maximal operator by M_\beta f(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac{r^\beta}{|B(x,r)|}\int_{B(x,r)}|f(y)|\,dy. Is it true that there exists a constant C=C(d,\beta)>0 such that, for every radial function f\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d), the function M_\beta f is weakly differentiable and satisfies \|\nabla M_\beta f\|_{L^q(\mathbb{R}^d)}\le C\|\nabla f\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)}?
justification: The draft is aiming at Question 8 of Section 5, which asks exactly whether the uncentered radial endpoint result in Theorem 5.3 also holds for the centered fractional maximal operator. The nearby context in Section 5 defines the centered fractional maximal operator, fixes the broader endpoint problem in Question 7, and presents Theorem 5.3 as the known uncentered radial result whose centered analogue is then asked in Question 8. So the sharp paper-faithful refinement is the centered analogue of Theorem 5.3, stated self-containedly with the operator definition, the endpoint exponent q=d/(d-\beta), radiality, weak differentiability, and the L^q gradient estimate.
